title: This Is the Best-Performing Magnificent Seven Stock of 2026. Is It Still a Buy?

This Is the Best-Performing Magnificent Seven Stock of 2026. Is It Still a Buy?
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool

AAPL

The "Magnificent Seven" is a grouping of stocks used to describe some of the largest companies in the world that have helped lead the U.S. stock market higher over the past decade. It is made up of:

Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL)

Nvidia

Microsoft

Alphabet

Amazon

Meta Platforms

Tesla

For U.S.-listed stocks, all seven of these are in the top 10, so being on this list is a big deal. However, 2026 hasn't been the greatest year for the Magnificent Seven. The S&P 500 is up about 12.3% this year, and only three stocks are outperforming it: Apple, Amazon, and Microsoft. But which one of these is doing the best? It's the non-AI one.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Apple leads all Magnificent Seven stocks

The top performer so far in 2026 has been Apple, up about 29%. That's practically double the second-best performer, Amazon, which has risen around 15%. So, what has separated Apple from the competition? I think there are two reasons.

First, Apple really isn't an AI stock. While its products have some AI features, it's not spending hundreds of billions of dollars on data centers like every other company on this list (besides Nvidia, which is selling the equipment for these data centers). As a whole, the market has been a bit bearish on the AI buildout lately, and Apple has been a haven for investors who aren't as keen on the long-term prospects of AI.

In fact, Apple is the only stock among the top 10 largest companies on U.S. exchanges that doesn't have significant AI investments or business cases riding on the AI buildout. This has made it a safe haven for non-AI investors and has boosted its stock.

Another reason Apple has done well this year is that its iPhone 17 lineup was the most popular of any of its previous models. This has driven sales growth and has made Apple a respectable business again.

However, Apple's day of reckoning could be coming. Outside of Tesla (which has a sky-high valuation of 424 times trailing earnings), Apple is by far the most expensive stock in the Magnificent Seven.

NVDA PE Ratio data by YCharts

As a result, I think the stock could be getting a bit too pricey, and investors need to watch out. Apple's strong performance this year hasn't come entirely from business results, and if the market flips its stance on AI and becomes bullish on it again, Apple's stock could sell off in favor of some AI-focused investments. It's about as good as it gets for Apple sentiment right now. As a result, I don't think Apple stock is a buy right now.

title: Banks ban AI from accounts over fears of rogue agents
detail:
Banks ban AI from accounts over fears of rogue agents
Tom Saunders
Sun, November 8, 2026 at 12:50 AM CST 4 min read
META
Trade META on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Britain's biggest banks have banned AI agents from accessing customer accounts over fears that personal finance bots will go rogue.

HSBC, Nationwide, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds have all moved to block AI agents, including in some cases specific bans on making transactions on a customer's behalf without their direct involvement.

AI agents that can manage people's money – and their personal lives – are seen as one of the most promising frontiers for the technology.

However, banks are concerned that bots could go rogue and mismanage people's money, with no clear rules as to who would be responsible in that scenario. Lenders are also concerned that en masse, bot-enabled switches could also threaten profits and, in a worst-case scenario, financial stability.

In September, Mark Zuckerberg's Meta launched Muse, a personal AI assistant that can carry out tasks such as shopping and managing bills for users. The app, which has not yet launched in the UK but is expected to, has topped download charts in North America.

Rather than just providing advice, AI agents such as Muse will carry out tasks such as sending emails or ordering shopping. Increasingly in the US, customers are directing their agents to manage their savings directly in their bank accounts.

Similar products are expected in Britain. Anne Boden, the founder of Starling Bank, has argued that AI should be entrusted with people's finances and recently announced on LinkedIn that she was hiring engineers for a new startup which would be "right at the start of the next revolution in banking technology".

Bank bosses are concerned that bots could go rogue, following a series of incidents outside the financial system in which AI has accessed systems without authorisation.

Manus Costello, the chief financial officer at Standard Chartered, said last week: "We need to be very careful that those tools are safe for customers and safe for us before we allow them in."

Will Chalmers, the chief financial officer of Lloyds, said recently the bank had not seen any sign of AI agents accessing bank accounts but added: "We do guard against that type of risk, and we take it very seriously."

The Financial Conduct Authority is working with the City and other regulators to develop rules to govern AI agents in finance.

Sources close to the regulator said it was up to the banks to make decisions on AI access but added that early research showed that agents could behave in unexpected ways.

The bans from UK banks are understood to be pre-emptive, with no signs yet that AI bots are accessing accounts.

title: Apple Completes the Set: Every Magnificent Seven Stock Opts Out of OKX-ICE Venue

Apple Completes the Set: Every Magnificent Seven Stock Opts Out of OKX-ICE Venue
Decrypt Staff

META
AAPL
MSFT
GOOG
AMZN
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Every member of Wall Street's "Magnificent Seven" now wants its stock kept off OKX and ICE's planned tokenized stock venue.

Apple and Meta Platforms are among 11 companies added to the list of objecting issuers in an updated notice from OKXICE TSV dated Thursday.

They join Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia and Tesla, completing a sweep by the group of tech giants that makes up a large share of the S&P 500's value. The other new objectors are Home Depot, Boeing, GE Vernova, Palantir, ServiceNow, S&P Global, KLA, Super Micro Computer and Nebius Group, bringing the total number of companies saying "no" to the OKX and ICE platform to 67.

Meta's objection carries some irony. The Facebook parent once tried to launch its own stablecoin, Libra, later renamed Diem, before abandoning the project in 2022 amid regulatory pushback.

Apple had been one of the last megacaps missing from the list after Amazon, Tesla, and SpaceX objected in the venue's Nov. 2 notice. The tally stood at 56 then, and at nine on Oct. 15, when the first objectors appeared.

Just as notable is who hasn't objected. Crypto-friendly public companies such as Coinbase, Robinhood and Strategy don't appear on the list. Coinbase launched tokenized stocks for non-U.S. users on its Base network in August. Berkshire Hathaway, Visa, and Exxon Mobil are also absent. It's unclear whether OKXICE notified those companies.

Under the SEC's innovation exemption, which the agency unveiled in September after the Clarity Act failed to advance in the Senate, a venue must notify a company before offering a version of its shares tokenized by an unaffiliated third party. If the company objects in writing within 30 days, the venue can't make that stock available for trading, according to the SEC's order. It's worth noting, though, that the objection applies only to that venue.

OKXICE TSV, a 50-50 joint venture between NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange and OKX's U.S. holding company, plans to offer tokenized U.S. stocks 24/7 through permissioned pools on OKX's XLayer blockchain. An outside "tokenizer" would hold real shares one-for-one through a registered broker-dealer.

With the market's biggest names opted out, it's unclear which major stocks the venue will be able to offer at launch, and its notices don't list the tokens it plans to make available.
